title: The Silence Before and After a Sound
script: This is Door 17. The Silence Before and After a Sound. It is verse 40 of the old text. In our plain words: whoever rests in the silence before a sound begins, and after it ends, becomes open space, the old text says, through the power of that silence. Jaideva Singh, the translator the school follows, reads it as resting in the empty moment before a syllable is spoken and after it is spoken. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep any sound soft. There is no need to raise the voice. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the place to rest. It is the silence just before a sound, and the silence just after it. Let the sound be small, and the silences large. [pause 3s] Breathe in easily, for about four. On some out-breaths, about six, say one soft syllable, such as ma, and let it end with the breath. On the others, just breathe out. Don't stop the breath. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 20s] Before the sound, notice the quiet it comes out of. After it, stay in the quiet it goes back into. [pause 20s] There is no need to strain to hear. The silence is already there. [pause 20s] Let the syllable go now. Rest in the silence that is left. [pause 16s] Release the attention. Feel the weight of the body on its support. Open the eyes when ready.

title: Following a Long Musical Note to Its End
script: This is Door 18. Following a Long Musical Note to Its End. It is verse 41 of the old text. In our plain words: listen with an undivided mind to a long note from a stringed instrument, or any long sound, and follow it as it unfolds. At its very end, the old text says, you become a body of open space. Singh says a good note seems to come out of silence and go back into it, and the mind can stay with the echo instead of wandering. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep the volume comfortable. Don't put your ear close to a loud instrument. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or rest them on the instrument. [pause 4s] You need one long note: a plucked string, a singing bowl, or a recorded drone. Play it now, or have it ready to play once each round. Follow it to its last trace. When you can't hear it any more, don't move on. Stay in what is left. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Sound the note. Follow it as it thins. Stay where it ends. [pause 16s] Another note, if you like. Listen with your whole attention, all the way to the edge. [pause 16s] Let the count go. After the last note ends, rest in the space it leaves. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: Sounding a Seed-Mantra into Silence
script: This is Door 19. Sounding a Seed-Mantra into Silence. It is verse 42 of the old text. In our plain words: sound a compact seed-sound, a mantra, through its spoken letters, then follow it into its finer stages, the hum and the fading echo, all the way into silence. Then, the old text says, you become Shiva, its name for the divine. The verse means any such seed-sound. The school uses Om, said as A, U, M. Singh's commentary maps the fine stages onto places in the body; we leave that map in the books. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep the voice soft and the out-breath easy. Take a free breath between rounds whenever you need one. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the path of the sound. First the letters, A, U, M. Then the hum. Then a fading echo. Then silence. The silence at the end is where you rest. [pause 3s] Breathe in easily, for about four. Let the out-breath, about eight, carry a soft A-U-M that turns into a hum and fades. Aloud, or silently. If eight is too long, make it shorter and let the breath finish. Never strain. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 24s] Follow it from voice, to hum, to silence. Rest there until the next in-breath comes by itself. [pause 24s] Loud, then faint, then gone. You don't need to make the silence. It is already there. [pause 24s] Let the sound rest now. Stay with the silence. [pause 12s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: Space in Every Direction at Once, Within the Body
script: This is Door 20. Space in Every Direction at Once, Within the Body. It is verse 43 of the old text. In our plain words: feel space within your own body, in every direction at once. When the mind is free of busy thoughts, the old text says, everything becomes space. Singh stresses two things: all directions together, not one after another, and a quiet mind. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If the openness feels unsettling, open your eyes and feel your body touching the floor. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the space inside the body. Front, back, both sides, up and down. Not one by one. All of them at once, opening together. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Space opening in every direction at once, inside the body. [pause 16s] If a thought comes, let it pass. Don't follow it. The openness stays simple. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the openness. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: The Void Above and the Void at the Base
script: This is Door 21. The void above and the void at the base. It is verse 44 of the old text. In our plain words: feel the empty space above you and the empty space at the base of the body, at the same moment. Then, the old text says, the mind becomes empty of thoughts. The old word for 'above' can also mean 'back', but Singh, Wallis and Baumer all read it as above. The school follows them. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep your attention light. There is nothing to push or lift. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now two spaces. One just above the head. One at the base of the body. Feel both together, at the same moment. Don't go back and forth. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] The space above, and the space at the base, both at once. [pause 16s] The mind between them may grow quiet. Let it. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Stay with both spaces lightly. [pause 16s] Release the attention. Feel the weight of the body on its support. Open the eyes when ready.

title: Three Voids at Once: Above, Base and Heart
script: This is Door 22. Three voids at once: above, base and heart. It is verse 45 of the old text. In our plain words: steadily feel three empty spaces at once: above the head, at the base, and in the heart. Because no thought is building there, the old text says, the thought-free state arises. Singh reports an old reading: the space above stands for the knower, the space at the base for what is known, and the heart for knowing itself. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If keeping three places feels like effort, go back to two, as in Door 21, or to one. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now three spaces. Just above the head. In the centre of the chest. At the base of the body. Feel all three together, steadily. Don't move between them. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Above, heart, base. All three at once. [pause 16s] Steady and easy. The quiet may come by itself. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest with the three spaces together. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: A Moment of Void in the Body
script: This is Door 23. A Moment of Void in the Body. It is verse 46 of the old text. In our plain words: even for a single moment, feel some part of the body as nothing but empty space, without thinking about it. Then, the old text says, you become free of busy thought. Singh reads 'part of the body' as the whole body taken as the small self. Wallis and Baumer read it as any part, such as a hand. The school follows Wallis and Baumer. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep it brief and light. If numbness or unease comes, move your hand and feel it in the ordinary way. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Choose one hand. Feel it as it is. Then, for a moment, sense it as nothing but open space. Let the moment end by itself. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] For a moment, the hand as open space. Then let it be ordinary again. [pause 16s] Once more. Just a moment. No thinking about it. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the quiet those moments left. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: The Body's Tissues Pervaded by Space
script: This is Door 24. The Body's Tissues Pervaded by Space. It is verse 47 of the old text. In our plain words: feel everything the body is made of, bone, flesh and the rest, as filled through with space. Then, the old text says, the contemplation becomes steady. Singh says this helps someone who can't yet rest in emptiness directly. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If the picture feels unpleasant, imagine light or air passing through instead, or stop. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the body's tissues. Bone. Muscle. Blood. Skin. One after another, each one filled through with space, until the whole body feels open, like light through a sponge. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Bone, filled with space. Then muscle. [pause 16s] Blood, and skin, filled with space. The whole body open and porous. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in that openness. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: The Skin as a Wall with Nothing Inside
script: This is Door 25. The Skin as a Wall with Nothing Inside. It is verse 48 of the old text. In our plain words: think of the skin as a wall, with nothing at all inside it. Meditating like this, the old text says, you come to share in what can't be meditated on. Singh says we usually take ourselves to be the body, and this loosens that habit. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. If the picture feels unsettling, rest your attention on the breath or the feet instead. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Now the skin, all around the body. Feel it as a thin wall, like the walls of a room. And inside, nothing at all. Don't look for anything in there. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] A thin wall all around. Empty inside. [pause 16s] Rest in that emptiness. Nothing to find. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Stay with the thin wall and the empty room. [pause 16s] Release the attention. Feel the weight of the body on its support. Open the eyes when ready.

title: Senses Dissolved in the Space of the Heart
script: This is Door 26. Senses Dissolved in the Space of the Heart. It is verse 49 of the old text. In our plain words: let the senses settle into the space of the heart, in the middle of a lotus made of two bowls, with the mind on nothing else. Then, the old text says, you find the highest good fortune. Singh says the heart here is not the organ, but the centre of the chest, pictured as two bowls joined rim to rim. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. This is attention in the chest, not effort. Keep the breath free. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes. [pause 4s] Now the centre of the chest. Picture two shallow bowls meeting rim to rim, and a quiet space in the middle. Let the senses draw back from what they reach for, and settle there. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Sight, sound, touch, drawing back. Settling into the space between the bowls. [pause 16s] The mind on nothing else. Just this space. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Rest in the middle of the lotus. [pause 16s] Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: Mind Dissolved at the Dvādaśānta
script: This is Door 27. Mind dissolved at the dvadashanta. It is verse 50 of the old text. In our plain words: when the whole body is filled with awareness, and the mind dissolves in the dvadashanta, the goal, the old text says, becomes steadily present. Dvadashanta means 'the end of twelve': a point about twelve finger-widths from the body. Singh admits it is not clear which such point is meant here. He suggests the top of the head. The school uses a point at the crown, or just above it. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Keep your attention at the crown light. If pressure or a headache comes, move your attention to your feet. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] First, let awareness fill the whole body. Then let the mind rest at a small point at the crown of the head, or just above it. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] The whole body filled with awareness. The mind resting at the point above. [pause 16s] If the mind wanders, come back to the point. Gently. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Let the mind rest and dissolve there. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: Returning to the Dvādaśānta Wherever You Are
script: This is Door 28. Returning to the dvadashanta wherever you are. It is verse 51 of the old text. In our plain words: however and wherever you are, keep casting the mind into the dvadashanta, moment after moment. As the mind's restlessness thins, the old text says, something extraordinary arises within days. Dvadashanta means a point about twelve finger-widths from the body. Singh says it can be just above the head, or about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose, where the out-breath ends. This door is mostly practised in ordinary life. Here we rehearse it sitting. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. In daily life, keep your main attention on anything that needs it, like traffic or tools. This is a light return, not a withdrawal. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Sit as you are. A chair is good. Keep your eyes open. In daily life, this is done with the eyes open. [pause 4s] Choose the point: just above the head, or out in front of the nose where the out-breath ends. We will touch it for a moment, go back to looking at the room, and touch it again. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Touch the point for one breath. Then look at something in the room. [pause 16s] Back to the point. Then back to the room. Small returns, again and again. [pause 16s] Let the count go. Return once more, and carry on. [pause 16s] Keep the habit. Next time you wash your hands or wait for a door, return to the point for one breath.

title: The Fire of Time Rising Through One's Own Body
script: This is Door 29. The Fire of Time Rising Through One's Own Body. It is verse 52 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. In the old text, the practitioner imagines the body burnt up by the fire of time, rising from the foot. At the end, there is a tranquil radiance. Singh adds that a formula was spoken with it. He reads the image as all the limits of the body burning away, and only peace remaining. Imagining your own body burning can be distressing. So the school does not lead it. Anyone with trauma, a history of self-harm, or strong anxiety should leave this image alone. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 24. The body's tissues pervaded by space. There nothing burns. You feel bone and flesh gently filled with space, until the body feels open and calm. [pause 3s] Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.

title: The Whole World Burnt by the Fire of Time
script: This is Door 30. The Whole World Burnt by the Fire of Time. It is verse 53 of the old text. The school keeps this door as memory. We observe it. We do not practise it. In the old text, following the door before, the practitioner contemplates the whole world as burnt, with the mind on nothing else. Then, it says, the highest state of a person arises. Singh explains this as all limited things falling away, leaving the unlimited one who knows. Pictures of the world's destruction can be distressing, especially in anxious or grieving times. So the school does not lead it. [pause 4s] If you want a door to practise, go to Door 20. Space in every direction at once, within the body. There nothing is destroyed. You only feel space opening evenly, in every direction, inside you. [pause 3s] Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.

title: Principles Dissolving into Their Sources
script: This is Door 31. Principles Dissolving into Their Sources. It is verse 54 of the old text. In our plain words: meditate on the elements of your own body, or of the world, as dissolving one into the next, each finer than the last. At the end, the old text says, the supreme Goddess is revealed. Singh describes a long series of principles. The school uses a short form: solid, fluid, warmth, movement, space, and awareness. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Go slowly. If dissolving feels unsettling, stop at space and feel the floor. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Find any steady, easy position. A chair is good. The floor, with a cushion under you, is good. Lying down is good. Let the floor or the chair take your weight. Close your eyes, or lower them softly. [pause 4s] Six layers. Solid, like earth. Fluid, like water. Warmth, like fire. Movement, like air. Space. And awareness. Each one melts into the next. [pause 3s] Breathe naturally. About four in and four out, if counting helps; if not, don't count. Don't stop the breath, and don't stretch it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 16s] Feel the body's solidity. Let it soften into fluidity. Fluidity into warmth. [pause 16s] Warmth into movement. Movement into space. [pause 16s] Space into awareness. Let the count go, and rest in what remains. [pause 16s] Drop the exercise. Notice the room: its sounds, its light. Carry the quiet into what comes next.

title: Thick Breath, Thin Breath, Entering the Heart
script: This is Door 32. Thick Breath, Thin Breath, Entering the Heart. It is verse 55 of the old text. In our plain words: meditate on the breath as thick and then as thin, at the dvadashanta, and then enter the heart. Then, the old text says, you become free. Old readers differ on which place is thick and which is thin. Swami Lakshmanjoo read thick as audible, and thin as slow and quiet, often done while falling asleep. The school follows that plain reading, without any breath control. The dvadashanta here is the point in front of the nose where the out-breath ends. [pause 3s] If it hurts, stop. Never force the breath. If you feel light-headed, stop and breathe normally. If you feel dizzy, restless, or a strong feeling comes up, stop. Open your eyes, and rest your attention on your feet and the floor. Any steady, easy position. Lying down is natural for this door, since it can be done before sleep. A chair is good too. Close your eyes. [pause 4s] Two places. The point in front of the nose, where the out-breath ends. And the centre of the chest, the heart. [pause 3s] Breathe in for about four, and out for about six, softly enough that you can just hear it. Then let the breath grow quiet and slow by itself. Don't stop it. Six rounds, two at a time. [pause 20s] Soft, audible breaths. Attention out in front, where the out-breath ends. [pause 20s] Let the breath become thin and quiet on its own. Begin to let attention move into the heart. [pause 20s] Let the count go. Rest in the heart as the breath stays thin. [pause 16s] Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.
